critiques.issue: The tree is empty. There are no Lvl1 claims, so nothing can be supported or refuted, and later experiments will have no hypothesis to falsify. That invites ad-hoc tuning, with conclusions written up after the fact.
critiques.suggestion: Before the first run, write 3–5 Lvl1 claims about what drives wall-clock time at fixed accuracy. Suggested: H1, time is dominated by GPU compute per epoch (model FLOPs/throughput); H2, time is dominated by the number of epochs needed to reach 75% (sample efficiency: optimizer, schedule, label smoothing, augmentation); H3, fixed overheads in prepare/train (data loading on 4 CPUs, host-to-device copies, compile or first-iteration costs leaking into timed regions) are a large share; H4, the accuracy margin is variance-limited (seed spread forces over-training). Give each one a Lvl3 prediction with a numeric threshold.

critiques.issue: There are no results, not even the unmodified submission_template. Without a baseline, there is no reference time or accuracy and no picture of where the time goes.
critiques.suggestion: Make E001 the untouched template. Log accuracy, time, per-seed accuracy, and a breakdown of prepare vs train time and per-epoch time if the harness exposes it. Every later claim of an 'improvement' needs this anchor.

critiques.issue: With only 3 fixed seeds, accuracy differences of a few tenths of a percent, and time differences of a few percent from GPU or compile jitter, will look like real effects. The 0.753 cutoff is a 0.3 pp margin over 0.75. A recipe that lands at 0.752–0.756 is a coin flip, both here and on the 40-seed official run.
critiques.suggestion: Early on, run the baseline (or the first feasible recipe) 2–3 times to measure run-to-run variation in time and the per-seed accuracy std. Pre-register that a difference smaller than about 2σ is marked '~' (inconclusive). Treat any recipe below roughly 0.758 as fragile, not as a frontier point.

critiques.issue: The objective is to minimize time subject to a hard accuracy floor. A common failure is to optimize time first and then get stuck just under 0.753, or to over-shoot accuracy and waste time.
critiques.suggestion: First find any feasible recipe with comfortable headroom (~0.77). Then sweep the epoch count, the single largest lever, to map accuracy vs time and find the knee. Only after that, cut per-epoch cost. Record the accuracy-vs-epochs curve as an explicit Lvl3 prediction under H2.

critiques.target: Untried directions (prior-informed, to seed the tree)
critiques.issue: Known CIFAR speedrun techniques (airbench / hlb-cifar10 style) are not represented yet. Several of them carry over to CIFAR-100 but may behave differently with 100 classes.
critiques.suggestion: Candidate Lvl2 mechanisms to test: (a) whole dataset held on the GPU, with augmentation (flip, crop/translate) done on the GPU to avoid the 4-CPU dataloader bottleneck; (b) channels_last + bf16 autocast + torch.compile, with compile and warmup on synthetic data in build (untimed); (c) a small ResNet/airbench-style net, with width scaled for 100 classes; (d) label smoothing and a one-cycle/linear-decay LR schedule with Nesterov SGD or LAMB-like optimizers; (e) whitening-initialized first layer; (f) EMA or Lookahead; (g) progressive resizing or lower resolution early; (h) larger batch with LR scaling. Each should be a separate, falsifiable Lvl3 prediction.

critiques.issue: Cutting timed overhead is where the rules are easiest to break. Examples: preloading real data in build, caching a whitening init computed from real images outside prepare, letting state leak between trials (compiled-graph caches are fine, learned buffers are not), or running test-time augmentation or BN updates during eval.
critiques.suggestion: Add a compliance checklist to the notebook for any run that changes prepare/build. Specifically check: no real-data access in build or at import; full reset of params, buffers, optimizer, EMA and RNGs in prepare; eval is pure with a fixed model; and eval handles B=1..1024 within 5 s, including the compiled-shape recompile cost for odd batch sizes.

critiques.issue: Experiments run on an A100 SXM, but judging uses an A100 PCIe, which has a lower power and clock ceiling and is typically 10–20% slower on sustained compute. Rankings between recipes are probably preserved, but absolute times are not. The 600 s limit and the 5 s eval limit could matter for heavier recipes.
critiques.suggestion: Report time as a relative improvement over baseline, not as an absolute claim. Avoid recipes whose eval latency or per-trial time sits near a limit.

structured_output.summary: There's nothing to review yet: the hypothesis tree, results, predictions and notebook are all empty. No conclusions exist that could be contradicted or that rest on a single run, so the critiques above are about setting up the loop. (1) Run the unmodified template as E001 and record a time breakdown. (2) Measure run-to-run noise in time and accuracy before calling anything an improvement, and treat accuracy under ~0.758 as fragile given the 3-seed 0.753 cutoff. (3) Write Lvl1 claims about where time comes from now — compute per epoch, epochs needed, fixed overheads, seed variance — each with a numeric Lvl3 prediction. (4) Go for a comfortably feasible recipe first, then map the accuracy-vs-epochs curve. (5) Seed the tree with known speedrun techniques, kept as separate testable predictions: data and augmentation on the GPU, bf16 + channels_last + compile done in build, small ResNet/airbench nets, label smoothing, one-cycle schedules, whitening init, EMA, progressive resizing. (6) Keep a rule-compliance checklist for any overhead cut that touches build or prepare.
